title: A2/A3 FP32 and INT8 matmul with a contiguous bias row
surface: matmul(dst, a, b, m=, n=, k=, splitn=, splitk=, is_init=True, bias=) on A2/A3; Tensor(..., Position.L1, layout=Layout.ND) for the bias row; one kernel family across the a2 and a3 facades
study_for: `Layout.ND` on the bias tensor is what selects the A2 family's contiguous GM-to-L1 transfer. The operands are fractalized; the bias is a plain row, and saying so in the tensor declaration is how the staging is chosen. No padded A5-style transfer is substituted for it.

`is_init=True` is what makes split-K add the bias once. The `k=128` case runs eight passes, so a bias applied per pass would be eight times too large -- and because the values are exact, that failure is an exact multiple rather than a rounding difference. The failure output prints per-column deltas for the same reason: one delta per column points at the bias, a varying one at the product.

Split-N slices the bias row, and the two dtypes reach that differently. The INT32 bias already has the column addressing 32-element slices need; the FP32 bias gets there through an accepted same-width reinterpret to INT32 inside `matmul`, which keeps the addressing contiguous without converting any value. That asymmetry is the reason both dtypes have a split-N case.

The geometry constraints come from compact L1 storage with no implicit K padding: M a multiple of 16 in [16, 64], N one of 32/64/96, FP32 K a multiple of 16 and INT8 K a multiple of 32. The ten cases walk the minima, the maxima and a third N tile, so a path that only handled one tile or only even tile counts fails somewhere.

The bias is 3, 6, 9, ... -- distinct and increasing -- and `check_domain` asserts both. That is what makes a wrong N slice a wrong answer rather than the same one, and it is why the generator's choice of bias is part of the check rather than incidental.
do_not_copy_when: Your N is not 64 and you are using the no-split or split-K path. Both declare a static N=64 for the full bias row; only split-N takes an N argument.
You were going to convert the FP32 bias to INT32 to get column slicing. The reinterpret is at the same width and changes no value -- a conversion would change every one of them.

Your K is not aligned to its dtype's multiple. The L1 allocation here is compact, so there is no implicit padding to absorb a ragged K, and the guard refuses one rather than producing a plausible answer.
You need FP32 accumulation accuracy. Every operand is a dyadic eighth or a small integer, chosen so the product and the sum are exact. Nothing here generalises to real data.
